summary: Discusses how TLS and IPsec can secure SIGTRAN protocols and recommends the minimum security a node must implement. IPsec support is mandatory and TLS is optional.

plainLanguage.summary: The SIGTRAN protocols carry the messages that set up telephone calls, and they run over SCTP. This RFC says how those messages should be protected. Every node that runs SIGTRAN must support IPsec, and may also support TLS. It spells out what each of them has to do, from the cipher settings to the rules for connecting a peer.

questions: what is the starttls procedure for sigtran over sctp
subtitle: Which security the signaling-over-IP protocols must support: IPsec is mandatory, TLS is optional.

tldr.problem: The SIGTRAN protocols carry telephony signaling between switches, and that signaling used to travel on closed, physically protected networks, so there was no standard way to give it confidentiality or authentication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the minimum each node must implement: IPsec with ESP in transport mode, non-null encryption and IKE for key management, and with TLS as an optional alternative reached through a STARTTLS upgrade of the SCTP association.
tldr.outcome: IPsec support is mandatory for every SIGTRAN node and TLS support is optional, so an implementation can pick one of two ways to protect the signaling and still conform.

today:
RFC 3788 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that sets the minimum security for SIGTRAN nodes.

The memo itself is brief on its own security considerations: it says only that it discusses the usage of IPsec and TLS for securing SIGTRAN traffic. The requirements it states are unchanged by the document, so an implementation that supports IPsec with ESP in transport mode and IKE conforms to it, whether or not it also offers TLS.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
The SIGTRAN protocols are designed to carry signaling messages for telephony services. They are used between customer premises and service provider equipment in the case of the ISDN Q.921 User Adaptation Layer (IUA), and between service provider equipment only in the case of M2UA, M2PA, M3UA and SUA. The carriers may be different and may use other transport network providers, and the security requirements for these situations may differ.

SIGTRAN involves the security needs of several parties: the end-users of the services, the service providers and the applications involved. Additional security requirements may come from local regulation. The security needs overlap, but any solution should fulfil all of the different parties' needs. The SIGTRAN protocols assume that messages are secured by using either IPsec or TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: SIGTRAN is a family of protocols that carry the messages a telephone network uses to set up calls. This RFC works out how those messages should be protected, and settles on a single minimum that every implementation has to meet.

sections.title: Security in Telephony Networks
sections.content:
Security in telephony networks has mainly been based on the closed network principle. Two main protocols are used: access protocols such as ISDN for signaling in the access network, and the SS7 protocol stack in the core network. Because SS7 networks are often physically remote or inaccessible to the user, they are assumed to be protected from malicious users, equipment is often under lock and key, packet filtering is sometimes used at network boundaries between SS7 networks, and end-users are not directly connected to SS7 networks.

Access protocols are used for end-user signaling, and end-user signaling protocols are translated to SS7 based protocols by telephone switches run by network operators. Regulatory authorities often require SS7 switches with connections to different SS7 switches to be conformant to national or international test specifications. There are no standardised ways of using encryption technologies to provide confidentiality, or of using technologies for authentication. The description in the document applies both to telephony networks operated by a single operator and to several telephony networks connected and operated by different operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Telephone networks used to rely on their own physical security: the switching equipment was in locked rooms and the users could not reach it. That is why there was never a standard way to encrypt or authenticate this traffic. Moving the signaling onto IP means the protection has to be built into the protocols.

sections.title: Threats and Goals
sections.content:
The document divides Internet threats into two main types. Passive attacks happen when the attacker reads packets off the network but does not write them; examples given are confidentiality violations, password sniffing and offline cryptographic attacks. Active attacks are those where the attacker also writes data to the network; examples are replay attacks, message insertion, message deletion, message modification and man-in-the-middle attacks.

Internet protocols generally have communication security objectives, which are authentication of peers, integrity of user data transport, confidentiality of user data and replay protection, together with non-repudiation and system security, meaning the avoidance of unauthorised use, inappropriate use and denial of service. Communication security is mandatory in some network scenarios, and the main goal of the document is to recommend the minimum security means a SIGTRAN node must implement in order to attain secured communication.

All SIGTRAN protocols use SCTP as their transport protocol, and SCTP provides some transport related security features, such as resistance against blind denial of service attacks caused by flooding, masquerade and improper monopolisation of services. The document notes that there is no quick, one-size-fits-all solution for security. When a network using SIGTRAN protocols involves more than one party, it may not be reasonable to expect that all parties have implemented security in a sufficient manner, so end-to-end security should be the goal, and IPsec or TLS is recommended to ensure confidentiality of the user payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the network can either just listen or can also change what they see. The security a signaling protocol needs is therefore four things: knowing who is on the other end, knowing the messages were not altered, keeping the content secret, and refusing to replay an old message. This RFC works out the smallest set of mechanisms that delivers those four things.

sections.title: IPsec Usage
sections.content:
All SIGTRAN nodes using IPsec must implement IPsec ESP in transport mode with non-null encryption and authentication algorithms, to provide per-packet authentication, integrity protection and confidentiality, and must implement the replay protection mechanisms of IPsec. Where IP layer protection is needed, ESP in tunnel mode should be used, and non-null encryption should be used when using IPsec ESP.

All SIGTRAN nodes must support IKE for peer authentication, negotiation of security associations and key management, using the IPsec DOI. The implementations must support peer authentication using a pre-shared key, and may support certificate-based peer authentication using digital signatures. Peer authentication using the public key encryption methods in IKE's sections 5.2 and 5.3 should not be used. Conformant implementations must support IKE's Main Mode and Aggressive Mode. For transport mode with pre-shared keys, IKE Aggressive Mode should be used and Main Mode should not; when digital signatures are used, either may be used; and when ESP tunnel mode is used, IKE Main Mode may be used to create an ISAKMP association with identity protection during Phase 1.

When digital signatures are used, an IKE negotiator should use the IKE Certificate Request Payload to name the certification authorities trusted in accordance with its local policy, and should carry out pertinent certificate revocation checks before accepting a PKI certificate for use in IKE's authentication procedures. The Phase 2 Quick Mode exchanges used to negotiate protection for SIGTRAN sessions must explicitly carry the Identity Payload fields IDci and IDcr, and each Identity Payload must carry a single IP address and a single non-zero port number, and must not use the IP Subnet or IP Address Range formats. That lets the Phase 2 security association correspond to specific TCP and SCTP connections.

The document also notes that IPsec acceleration hardware may handle only a limited number of active IKE Phase 2 security associations, so Phase 2 delete messages may be sent for idle associations. The receipt of such a message should not be a reason to tear down a SIGTRAN session: it is preferable to leave the connection up, so that another Phase 2 association can be brought up if more traffic is sent. Because SCTP supports multi-homed hosts, one SCTP association can need several security associations, and IPsec implementations used by SIGTRAN nodes should support the IPsec feature described in RFC 3554.
sections.plainLanguage: When a node uses IPsec, it must use ESP in transport mode, with real encryption and a real integrity check on every packet, and it must reject packets it has already seen. Key management and peer authentication come from IKE, with a pre-shared key required and certificates optional. Each security association must name one IP address and one port, so that it protects one connection and not the whole host.

sections.title: TLS Usage
sections.content:
A SIGTRAN node that initiates a SCTP association acts as a TLS client, and a node that accepts a connection acts as a TLS server. Peers that implement TLS for security must mutually authenticate as part of TLS session establishment: the node acting as TLS server must request a certificate from the node acting as TLS client, and the node acting as TLS client must be prepared to supply one. RFC 3436 requires support of the cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and SIGTRAN nodes may negotiate other cipher suites.

TLS must be used on all bi-directional streams, and other uni-directional streams must not be used. A SCTP implementation used for TLS over SCTP must support fragmentation of user data and might also need to support the partial delivery API, even if all SIGTRAN messages are small. The unordered delivery feature of SCTP cannot be used together with TLS.

Because TLS only protects the payload, the SCTP header and all control chunks are not protected, which can be used for denial of service attacks. The SIGTRAN protocols use the same SCTP port number and payload protocol identifier when run over TLS, so a session upgrade procedure has to be used to start the TLS based communication. The procedure runs as follows.

  • If an ASP has been configured to use TLS, it sends a STARTTLS message on stream 0 and starts a timer T_TLS. This is the first message sent, and the ASP sends no other adaptation layer messages until the TLS based communication has been established.
  • If the peer does not support TLS, it sends back an ERROR message indicating an unsupported message type. The SCTP association is then terminated, and the management layer is told that the peer does not support TLS.
  • If the peer does support TLS, it sends back a STARTTLS_ACK message, and the client then starts TLS based communication.
  • If T_TLS expires without any of those answers, the association is terminated and the failure is reported to the management layer.

All SIGTRAN adaptation layers share a common message format. The STARTTLS message consists of a common header only, using message class 10 and message type 1, and the STARTTLS_ACK message uses the same class 10 with message type 2. Neither message contains any parameters. The document notes that this procedure makes it possible for a man-in-the-middle to cause a denial of service by claiming the peer does not support TLS, but that this kind of attack is always possible for a man-in-the-middle.
sections.plainLanguage: With TLS, the two nodes check each other's certificates when the connection is set up, and the connection is then protected from there on. Because the SIGTRAN messages travel over SCTP, the secure part has to be turned on after the connection exists: one side sends a STARTTLS message on stream 0, the other answers with an acknowledgement, and only then does the TLS handshake happen. If the peer does not answer, the connection is closed.

sections.title: Support of IPsec and TLS
sections.content:
If the content of SIGTRAN protocol messages is to be protected, either IPsec ESP or TLS can be used. In both the IPsec ESP transport mode case and the TLS case, the IP header information is neither encrypted nor protected. If IPsec ESP is chosen, the SCTP control information is encrypted and protected, whereas in the TLS based solution the SCTP control information is not encrypted and is only protected by SCTP procedures.

In general, both IPsec and TLS have enough mechanisms to secure SIGTRAN communications. So that a secured model works as soon as possible, the document makes one recommendation: a SIGTRAN node must support IPsec and may support TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Either mechanism protects the signaling itself, but they differ in how much of the surrounding traffic they cover. IPsec also encrypts the SCTP control information, while TLS leaves it readable. The requirement is the same either way: IPsec has to be there, TLS is a choice.

sections.title: Peer-to-Peer Considerations
sections.content:
M2PA, M3UA and SUA support the peer-to-peer model as a generalisation of the client-server model that IUA and M2UA support. A SIGTRAN node running one of those protocols in peer-to-peer mode is called a SIGTRAN peer. As with any peer-to-peer protocol, proper configuration of the trust model within a peer is essential to security. When certificates are used, the trust anchors trusted by the peer have to be configured, and they are likely to be unique to SIGTRAN usage and distinct from the trust anchors used for other purposes such as web browsing. In general the trust anchors are expected to be configured to reflect the business relationships between the organization hosting the peer and other organizations, so a peer will not typically be configured to allow connectivity with any arbitrary peer. When peers are not known beforehand, peer discovery may be required.

The document notes that IPsec is considerably less flexible than TLS when it comes to configuring trust anchors. Since the use of port identifiers is prohibited within IKE Phase 1, it is not possible to configure trusted trust anchors for each application individually within IPsec; the same policy must be used for all applications. A trust anchor trusted for use with a SIGTRAN protocol must therefore also be trusted to protect other protocols, for example SNMP. When pre-shared key authentication is used with IPsec, unique pre-shared keys are configured with peers identified by their IP address in Main Mode, or possibly their FQDN in Aggressive Mode, so the set of peers has to be known beforehand and peer discovery is typically not necessary.

It is recommended that SIGTRAN peers use the same security mechanism, IPsec or TLS, across all their sessions with other SIGTRAN peers, because inconsistent use can result in redundant mechanisms being used, for example TLS over IPsec, or worse, potential security vulnerabilities. When IPsec is used, a typical security policy for outbound traffic is "Initiate IPsec, from me to any, destination port P", and for inbound traffic "Require IPsec, from any to me, destination port P", where P is one of the registered port numbers for a SIGTRAN protocol. That policy causes IPsec to be used whenever a peer initiates a session and to be required whenever an inbound session occurs, and it is attractive because it does not require policy to be set for each peer or modified dynamically each time a new session is created.
sections.plainLanguage: In peer-to-peer mode, the two sides are equals, so each has to decide in advance which other parties it trusts. IPsec makes that harder than TLS does, because a policy cannot be written per application. The document advises picking one mechanism and using it for every session with a given peer, rather than mixing them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Message class 12 has been reserved in the Signaling User Adaptation Layer Assignments Registry. For that message class, message type 1 has been reserved for the STARTTLS message and message type 2 for the STARTTLS_ACK message.
sections.plainLanguage: The two messages that start the TLS upgrade have been given their own numbers in the registry of adaptation layer messages: a class for STARTTLS, and within it one number for the request and one for the acknowledgement.

items.title: Authentication of peers
items.text: Each node knows who is on the other end of the connection.

items.title: Integrity of user data
items.text: The receiver can tell that the message was not altered in transit.

items.title: Confidentiality of user data
items.text: The content of the message is not readable to anyone else.

items.title: Replay protection
items.text: A message that was already accepted cannot be sent again and accepted a second time.

items.title: Non-repudiation
items.text: A sender cannot later deny that it sent the message.

items.title: System security
items.text: Avoid unauthorised use, inappropriate use and denial of service.

messages.label: STARTTLS on stream 0
messages.note: The first message sent; the client starts the timer T_TLS and sends nothing else meanwhile.

messages.label: STARTTLS_ACK
messages.note: The peer supports TLS, so the client starts TLS based communication.

messages.label: TLS handshake
messages.note: The server must request a certificate, and the client must be ready to supply one.

cells: Not encrypted, protected only by SCTP procedures
